title: The Copernicus System
sub: A naked-eye star with five worlds
blurb: 55 Cancri is a quiet double star 41 light-years away in the constellation Cancer. Five planets circle its brighter sun — a family so notable that the star was formally named Copernicus in 2015, with its worlds named after the astronomers who first turned lenses on the sky.

title: The First Family of Five
sub: A full planetary system, found piece by piece
blurb: The worlds arrived one at a time: a hot Jupiter in 1996, then three more, and in 2007 a fifth — making 55 Cancri the first star beyond the Sun known to hold five planets. They crowd inward from a distant giant to a scorched world hugging the star.

title: A Jupiter of Its Own
sub: A giant on a wide, patient orbit
blurb: Far out at about 5.5 AU rides 55 Cancri d, a gas giant several times Jupiter's mass taking roughly fourteen years to round its star. When it was found in 2002 it was the first exoplanet known on an orbit as roomy as our own Jupiter's.

title: A Sun and a Distant Ember
sub: Two stars, a thousand AU apart
blurb: 55 Cancri A is a yellow star a little cooler and smaller than the Sun. Bound to it, but a thousand times further off than Earth is from the Sun, drifts a faint red dwarf — a companion so remote it takes millennia to complete a single lap.

title: You Can See It Yourself
sub: One of the few planet-hosting stars visible unaided
blurb: At magnitude 5.95 the star sits just inside the reach of the unaided eye. Under a truly dark sky, away from town lights, you can pick out that faint spark in Cancer and know that five worlds are circling it.

title: A World of Molten Rock
sub: 55 Cancri e, hot enough to melt stone
blurb: The innermost planet, 55 Cancri e, orbits so close that its daylit face reaches around 2,400 °C — far past the melting point of rock. Astronomers picture a super-Earth glowing beneath an ocean of magma, its surface never cooling enough to harden.

title: A Year in Eighteen Hours
sub: A whole orbit before your next sunrise
blurb: 55 Cancri e races around its star in about 17.7 hours, skimming a mere 0.015 AU above it — one twenty-fifth of Mercury's distance from the Sun. Fall asleep tonight and the planet will have lived a full year by the time you wake.

title: One Face, Forever
sub: Endless day on one side, endless night on the other
blurb: Held by its star's grip, 55 Cancri e almost certainly keeps one hemisphere turned starward for good. That side blazes white-hot while the far side sits in permanent darkness — yet it stays strangely warm, as though heat were being ferried across.

title: The Diamond Planet
sub: A dazzling idea that did not quite hold
blurb: In 2012 researchers suggested that a carbon-rich 55 Cancri e might hide a mantle of diamond beneath its crust, and the world made headlines. A sharper reading of the star's chemistry later found far less carbon than assumed — a beautiful hypothesis undone by better data.

title: Air Above the Magma
sub: A blanket bubbling up from an ocean of lava
blurb: In 2024 the JWST found the best evidence yet that this lava world holds an atmosphere — one rich in carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide, likely venting straight out of the magma below. It is the strongest sign we have of air on a rocky world beyond our own.

title: 41 Light-Years Away
sub: Close enough to study, far beyond reach
blurb: 55 Cancri lies about 41 light-years off in the constellation Cancer — near enough that our telescopes can weigh its planets and taste their air, yet so far that the light arriving tonight set out before anyone had found a single planet around another star.
